## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mahāsudassana Sutta* (DN 17) is the seventeenth discourse of the *Dīghanikāya* [SuttaCentral]. It serves as an expansion of an episode from the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16): when Ānanda laments that the Buddha intends to pass into final nirvana in Kusinārā, characterizing it as a remote jungle township, the Buddha explains that the city was once the magnificent capital Kusāvatī ruled by the legendary wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) Mahāsudassana [Norman 1983; Piya Tan 2004; Nattier 2008]. Having the character of a *jātaka*, the discourse identifies King Mahāsudassana as a past life of the Buddha [Anālayo 2010; Norman 1983]. The sutta details the king's earthly splendour, including the seven jewels of a universal monarch—the wheel, elephant, horse, gem, woman, treasurer, and counsellor—explaining that his greatness stemmed from his practice of generosity (*dāna*), self-control (*dama*), and self-restraint (*saṃyama*) [Tambiah 1984; Norman 1983; Piya Tan 2004]. King Mahāsudassana subsequently renounces his palace and wealth to cultivate meditative practice, specifically the four divine abodes (*brahma-vihāra*) [SuttaCentral; Gaffney 2003].
Scholars have noted that while the Theravāda tradition transmits the *Mahāsudassana Sutta* as an independent sutta following DN 16, Sanskrit and other northern versions commonly integrate the *Mahāsudarśana* narrative directly within the *Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra* [Norman 1983; Radich 2011; Revire 2016]. Parallel recensions identified by SuttaCentral include the Chinese *Dīrghāgama* (DĀ 2), the *Madhyama Āgama* parallel *Da Shanjian wang jing* (MĀ 68 / T 26.68), several individual Chinese translations (T 5, T 6, T 7, T 1451.37), Sanskrit manuscript fragments (SF 102, SF 245), and the Pali *Mahāsudassana Jātaka* (Ja 95) [SuttaCentral; Nattier 2008]. In DharmaNexus, the text exhibits extensive Pali-internal reuse with the *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), *Bālapaṇḍita Sutta* (MN 129), *Maghadeva Sutta* (MN 83), *Cakkavatti Sutta* (DN 26), and *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16), alongside cross-language alignment with the Sanskrit *Mahāparinirvāṇasūtra*, the *Lalitavistara*, and Tibetan Vinaya texts [DharmaNexus]. Modern scholars have also studied the text's lavish cosmic descriptions in relation to the origins of Pure Land depictions of Sukhāvatī [Goldstone 1978; Halkias 2013].
